items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The amount by which government revenue exceeds government expenditure in a given year"?
items.answer: budget surplus
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of budget surplus.

items.stem: Explain why indirect taxes are often regressive.
items.answer: Low-income households spend a larger proportion of their income on taxed goods, so the tax represents a larger share of their income.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Low-income households spend a larger proportion of their income on taxed goods, so the tax represents a larger share of their income. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between direct taxes and indirect taxes.
items.answer: Direct taxes are levied on income and wealth and paid directly by the taxpayer (income tax); indirect taxes are levied on spending and collected through sellers (VAT).
items.markingKey: Direct taxes are levied on income and wealth and paid directly by the taxpayer (income tax); indirect taxes are levied on spending and collected through sellers (VAT). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The budget statement of Tarsia shows tax and other receipts of $260 bn and total public spending of $312 bn, with nominal GDP of $650 bn. Calculate the budget balance and state whether it is a deficit or a surplus.
items.answer: Balance = 260 − 312 = −$52 bn: a budget deficit.
items.markingKey: Revenue − expenditure = 260 − 312 = -52. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for −$52 bn (deficit). Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant.

items.stem: With reference to the UK budget deficit in 2020-21, explain how it illustrates the government budget and deficits.
items.answer: UK public sector net borrowing reached about 15% of GDP in 2020-21, the highest since the Second World War, because of the furlough scheme and lower tax revenue. A collapse in revenue and large emergency spending created a record peacetime deficit
items.markingKey: Context (UK public sector net borrowing reached about 15% of GDP in 2020-21, the highest since the Second World War, because of the furlough scheme and lower tax revenue.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A collapse in revenue and large emergency spending created a record peacetime deficit – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the government budget and deficits.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that governments should always aim to balance their budgets.
items.answer: Budgets should be balanced over the cycle rather than every year, allowing deficits in recessions and surpluses in booms.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: avoids growing debt and interest payments; reduces crowding out; builds credibility with markets. Arguments against: prevents automatic stabilisers from working; deficits are appropriate in recessions; borrowing for productive investment raises future growth. Supported judgement: Budgets should be balanced over the cycle rather than every year, allowing deficits in recessions and surpluses in booms.

items.stem: Which of the following is a source of government revenue?
options: Income from state-owned enterprises and the sale of assets
items.answer: Income from state-owned enterprises and the sale of assets
items.markingKey: B. Besides taxes, governments earn revenue from SOEs and privatisation.

items.stem: Explain why governments distinguish between current and capital expenditure.
items.answer: Capital spending creates assets that raise future productive capacity and can generate future revenue, so borrowing for it is easier to justify than borrowing for day-to-day current spending.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Capital spending creates assets that raise future productive capacity and can generate future revenue, so borrowing for it is easier to justify than borrowing for day-to-day current spending. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Omar writes: "A budget surplus means the government has no debt." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A surplus means revenue exceeds spending this year; the stock of debt from past deficits remains, though a surplus can be used to reduce it.
items.markingKey: A surplus means revenue exceeds spending this year; the stock of debt from past deficits remains, though a surplus can be used to reduce it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that transfer payments are counted as government spending (G) in aggregate demand. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Transfers redistribute income and are not payment for current output, so they are excluded from G; they affect AD indirectly through consumption.
items.markingKey: Transfers redistribute income and are not payment for current output, so they are excluded from G; they affect AD indirectly through consumption. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why might a cut in income tax have a smaller effect on AD than an equal rise in government spending?
options: Part of the tax cut is saved or spent on imports
Taxes do not affect disposable income
Tax cuts have no effect on AD
items.answer: Part of the tax cut is saved or spent on imports
items.markingKey: B. Only the MPC share is spent in the first round.

items.stem: "A tax cut and an equal increase in government spending always have the same effect on AD." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Part of a tax cut is saved or spent on imports, so the first-round injection is smaller; an equal rise in G usually has a larger multiplier effect.
items.markingKey: Part of a tax cut is saved or spent on imports, so the first-round injection is smaller; an equal rise in G usually has a larger multiplier effect. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between automatic stabilisers and discretionary fiscal policy.
items.answer: Discretionary policy involves deliberate decisions to change spending or tax rates; automatic stabilisers change tax revenue and benefit spending automatically with the business cycle.
items.markingKey: Discretionary policy involves deliberate decisions to change spending or tax rates; automatic stabilisers change tax revenue and benefit spending automatically with the business cycle. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe China's 2008 stimulus package and explain what it reveals about fiscal policy and AD.
items.answer: In November 2008 China announced a 4 trillion yuan stimulus (about 12% of GDP) focused on infrastructure. Large spending on railways and roads sustained growth above 9% in 2009, though it raised local government debt
items.markingKey: Context (In November 2008 China announced a 4 trillion yuan stimulus (about 12% of GDP) focused on infrastructure.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large spending on railways and roads sustained growth above 9% in 2009, though it raised local government debt – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to fiscal policy and AD.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the effect of expansionary fiscal policy on a deflationary gap in the Keynesian model, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Keynesian AS; AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2 through higher G or lower taxes; on the horizontal/upward-sloping section, real GDP rises towards Yf with little rise in the price level; multiplier amplifies the shift.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Keynesian AS; AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2 through higher G or lower taxes; on the horizontal/upward-sloping section, real GDP rises towards Yf with little rise in the price level; multiplier amplifies the shift. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that expansionary fiscal policy is the most effective way to end a recession.
items.answer: Fiscal policy is most effective in deep recessions with low interest rates and spare capacity, especially when well targeted and temporary.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: directly raises AD; multiplier effects; effective when monetary policy is at the zero lower bound; can target sectors and regions; infrastructure raises LRAS. Arguments against: time lags in planning and approval; crowding out; rising debt and interest burdens; may be politically hard to reverse. Supported judgement: Fiscal policy is most effective in deep recessions with low interest rates and spare capacity, especially when well targeted and temporary.

items.stem: Explain how expansionary fiscal policy can reduce cyclical unemployment.
items.answer: Higher G or lower taxes increase AD directly and through the multiplier; firms increase output and, since labour is a derived demand, hire more workers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher G or lower taxes increase AD directly and through the multiplier; firms increase output and, since labour is a derived demand, hire more workers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why fiscal policy can affect both AD and LRAS.
items.answer: Spending on infrastructure, education and health raises AD in the short run and increases productive capacity (LRAS) in the long run.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Spending on infrastructure, education and health raises AD in the short run and increases productive capacity (LRAS) in the long run. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using the US CARES Act (2020) as an example, explain expansionary fiscal policy.
items.answer: The $2.2 trillion CARES Act in March 2020 included direct payments to households, expanded unemployment benefits and loans to firms. The package supported household incomes and AD during lockdowns, helping a rapid recovery in consumption
items.markingKey: Context (The $2.2 trillion CARES Act in March 2020 included direct payments to households, expanded unemployment benefits and loans to firms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "automatic stabilisers"?
options: A tax on spending on goods and services, such as VAT or excise duties, collected from sellers
Features of the tax and benefit system, such as progressive taxes and unemployment benefits, that automatically reduce fluctuations in AD over the business cycle
The amount by which government revenue exceeds government expenditure in a given year
The reduction in private investment (and consumption) caused by higher government borrowing that raises interest rates
items.answer: Features of the tax and benefit system, such as progressive taxes and unemployment benefits, that automatically reduce fluctuations in AD over the business cycle
items.markingKey: B. "automatic stabilisers" is features of the tax and benefit system, such as progressive taxes and unemployment benefits, that automatically reduce fluctuations in AD over the business cycle.

items.stem: Explain the difference between crowding out and crowding in.
items.answer: Crowding out is the reduction in private spending caused by government borrowing raising interest rates; crowding in is when government spending, especially on infrastructure in a recession, raises confidence and profitability, increasing private investment.
items.markingKey: Crowding out is the reduction in private spending caused by government borrowing raising interest rates; crowding in is when government spending, especially on infrastructure in a recession, raises confidence and profitability, increasing private investment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between crowding in and crowding out.
items.answer: Crowding out is the reduction in private spending caused by government borrowing raising interest rates; crowding in is when government spending, especially on infrastructure in a recession, raises confidence and profitability, increasing private investment.
items.markingKey: Crowding out is the reduction in private spending caused by government borrowing raising interest rates; crowding in is when government spending, especially on infrastructure in a recession, raises confidence and profitability, increasing private investment. items.stem: A student claims that automatic stabilisers require the government to pass new laws in each recession. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They work automatically through existing tax and benefit rules; no new decision is needed.
items.markingKey: They work automatically through existing tax and benefit rules; no new decision is needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A government increases spending by $20 bn when the economy is close to full employment, financed by borrowing. Explain two ways in which its effect on real GDP may be smaller than expected.
items.answer: Crowding out: higher borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment and consumption. Near full employment the AS curve is steep, so much of the AD increase raises the price level rather than output; time lags may also delay the effect.
items.markingKey: Crowding out: higher borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment and consumption. Near full employment the AS curve is steep, so much of the AD increase raises the price level rather than output; time lags may also delay the effect.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that automatic stabilisers are more useful than discretionary fiscal policy for stabilising the economy.
items.answer: Automatic stabilisers are the first line of defence, but large shocks require timely, temporary and targeted discretionary measures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no recognition or decision lags; no political bargaining; reverse automatically in booms. Arguments against: too small to offset deep shocks such as 2008 or 2020; cannot target specific sectors; weaker in countries with small welfare states. Supported judgement: Automatic stabilisers are the first line of defence, but large shocks require timely, temporary and targeted discretionary measures.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "automatic stabilisers".
items.answer: Features of the tax and benefit system, such as progressive taxes and unemployment benefits, that automatically reduce fluctuations in AD over the business cycle

items.stem: Briefly explain why crowding out may reduce the effectiveness of expansionary fiscal policy.
items.answer: Higher government borrowing increases the demand for loanable funds, raising interest rates; private investment and interest-sensitive consumption fall, offsetting some of the rise in G.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher government borrowing increases the demand for loanable funds, raising interest rates; private investment and interest-sensitive consumption fall, offsetting some of the rise in G. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which automatic stabilisers in Germany in 2009 shows automatic stabilisers.
items.answer: Germany's Kurzarbeit (short-time work) scheme supported about 1.5 million workers at its peak in 2009, and unemployment barely rose despite a 5.7% fall in GDP. Payments to workers on reduced hours automatically supported incomes and AD while keeping workers attached to firms
items.markingKey: Context (Germany's Kurzarbeit (short-time work) scheme supported about 1.5 million workers at its peak in 2009, and unemployment barely rose despite a 5.7% fall in GDP.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Mateo writes: "Any debt above 60% of GDP will cause a crisis." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sustainability depends on interest rates, growth, who holds the debt and the currency; Japan has very high debt without a crisis, while some countries defaulted at much lower levels.
items.markingKey: Sustainability depends on interest rates, growth, who holds the debt and the currency; Japan has very high debt without a crisis, while some countries defaulted at much lower levels. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a downgrade in a country's credit rating can make its debt problem worse.
items.answer: Investors demand higher yields to hold riskier bonds, raising debt-servicing costs and widening the deficit, which can further raise the debt ratio. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Investors demand higher yields to hold riskier bonds, raising debt-servicing costs and widening the deficit, which can further raise the debt ratio. items.stem: Briefly describe the Greek debt crisis and explain what it reveals about consequences of unsustainable government debt.
items.answer: Greek government debt exceeded 170% of GDP by 2011; Greece needed three bailouts (2010, 2012, 2015) and a restructuring that imposed losses of over 50% on private creditors in 2012. Loss of market confidence raised borrowing costs to unaffordable levels, forcing austerity and default
items.markingKey: Context (Greek government debt exceeded 170% of GDP by 2011; Greece needed three bailouts (2010, 2012, 2015) and a restructuring that imposed losses of over 50% on private creditors in 2012.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Loss of market confidence raised borrowing costs to unaffordable levels, forcing austerity and default – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to consequences of unsustainable government debt.

items.stem: Sundara has public debt of $550 bn and GDP of $500 bn. Over the next year nominal GDP is forecast to rise by 6%, and the deficit is projected at 5% of next year's GDP. Calculate the debt-to-GDP ratio at the start and at the end of the year, and explain whether the debt is becoming more or less sustainable.
items.answer: Start: 110.0%; deficit = $26.5 bn, end debt $576.5 bn, GDP $530.0 bn → 108.8%. The ratio falls, because nominal GDP grows faster than debt, so debt is becoming more sustainable.
items.markingKey: 550/500 = 110.0%; new GDP 530.0; deficit 26.5; debt 576.5; ratio 108.8%. [M1] for correct method/working; [A1] for both ratios. Award [A1] only with correct units/notation where relevant. [R1] link between deficit, growth and the ratio.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that high government debt is a serious threat to an economy.
items.answer: High debt is risky if it is in foreign currency, held by foreigners and rising faster than GDP; otherwise gradual stabilisation is preferable to rapid austerity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rising interest payments crowd out public services; risk of loss of confidence and crisis; burden on future generations. Arguments against: debt used for investment can raise growth; own-currency debt with low interest rates is manageable; reducing debt too quickly can cause recession (austerity). Supported judgement: High debt is risky if it is in foreign currency, held by foreigners and rising faster than GDP; otherwise gradual stabilisation is preferable to rapid austerity.

items.stem: A student claims that government debt is like household debt and must always be fully repaid. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Governments can roll over debt indefinitely, borrowing anew to repay maturing bonds; what matters is whether the debt-to-GDP ratio is stable and servicing costs are manageable.

items.stem: Distinguish between unsustainable debt and sustainable debt.

items.answer: In a boom, incomes rise and people move into higher bands, so tax revenue rises faster than income, restraining consumption; in a recession revenue falls faster, cushioning disposable income.

items.stem: Briefly describe Norway's budget surpluses and explain what it reveals about budget surpluses.
items.answer: Norway has run large budget surpluses for decades and saves oil revenue in its sovereign wealth fund, worth over $1.7 trillion (about 20,000 billion kroner) in 2025. Revenue from oil exceeds government spending, so surpluses are invested for future generations
items.markingKey: Context (Norway has run large budget surpluses for decades and saves oil revenue in its sovereign wealth fund, worth over $1.7 trillion (about 20,000 billion kroner) in 2025.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Revenue from oil exceeds government spending, so surpluses are invested for future generations – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to budget surpluses.

items.stem: With reference to automatic stabilisers in Germany in 2009, explain how it illustrates automatic stabilisers.
items.answer: Germany's Kurzarbeit (short-time work) scheme supported about 1.5 million workers at its peak in 2009, and unemployment barely rose despite a 5.7% fall in GDP. Payments to workers on reduced hours automatically supported incomes and AD while keeping workers attached to firms
items.markingKey: Context (Germany's Kurzarbeit (short-time work) scheme supported about 1.5 million workers at its peak in 2009, and unemployment barely rose despite a 5.7% fall in GDP.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Payments to workers on reduced hours automatically supported incomes and AD while keeping workers attached to firms – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to automatic stabilisers.

items.stem: "Government debt is like household debt and must always be fully repaid." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Governments can roll over debt indefinitely, borrowing anew to repay maturing bonds; what matters is whether the debt-to-GDP ratio is stable and servicing costs are manageable.
items.markingKey: Governments can roll over debt indefinitely, borrowing anew to repay maturing bonds; what matters is whether the debt-to-GDP ratio is stable and servicing costs are manageable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the effect of contractionary fiscal policy on an inflationary gap.
items.answer: AD/AS: lower G or higher taxes shift AD left; output falls back to Yp and inflationary pressure is reduced.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: AD/AS: lower G or higher taxes shift AD left; output falls back to Yp and inflationary pressure is reduced. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: "A budget surplus means the government has no debt." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A surplus means revenue exceeds spending this year; the stock of debt from past deficits remains, though a surplus can be used to reduce it.
items.markingKey: A surplus means revenue exceeds spending this year; the stock of debt from past deficits remains, though a surplus can be used to reduce it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to crowding out debates in the USA after 2023, explain how it illustrates crowding out.
items.answer: With US federal deficits around 6% of GDP in 2023-24, ten-year Treasury yields rose above 4.5%, prompting warnings of crowding out of private investment. Large borrowing near full employment competes for loanable funds, raising interest rates and reducing private investment
items.markingKey: Context (With US federal deficits around 6% of GDP in 2023-24, ten-year Treasury yields rose above 4.5%, prompting warnings of crowding out of private investment.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large borrowing near full employment competes for loanable funds, raising interest rates and reducing private investment – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to crowding out.

items.stem: Using Sri Lanka's default in 2022 as an example, explain debt in foreign currency.
items.answer: Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt in May 2022 after foreign exchange reserves ran out, causing shortages of fuel, food and medicine. Without foreign reserves the government could not service dollar-denominated debt, leading to default and a severe recession
items.markingKey: Context (Sri Lanka defaulted on its foreign debt in May 2022 after foreign exchange reserves ran out, causing shortages of fuel, food and medicine.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without foreign reserves the government could not service dollar-denominated debt, leading to default and a severe recession – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to debt in foreign currency.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Expansionary fiscal policy is the most effective way to end a recession."
items.answer: Fiscal policy is most effective in deep recessions with low interest rates and spare capacity, especially when well targeted and temporary.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: directly raises AD; multiplier effects; effective when monetary policy is at the zero lower bound; can target sectors and regions; infrastructure raises LRAS. Arguments against: time lags in planning and approval; crowding out; rising debt and interest burdens; may be politically hard to reverse. Supported judgement: Fiscal policy is most effective in deep recessions with low interest rates and spare capacity, especially when well targeted and temporary.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Deliberate changes in government spending or taxation decided by the government"?
items.answer: discretionary fiscal policy
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of discretionary fiscal policy.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "capital expenditure".
items.answer: Government spending on assets such as roads, schools and hospitals that add to the capital stock
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: government spending on assets such as roads, schools and hospitals that add to the capital stock. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Crowding out occurs when:
items.answer: government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment
items.markingKey: government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment. Competition for loanable funds.

items.stem: Explain why debt in a foreign currency is riskier than debt in the domestic currency.
items.answer: If the domestic currency depreciates, the value of foreign-currency debt rises in domestic terms, and the government cannot print foreign currency to repay it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If the domestic currency depreciates, the value of foreign-currency debt rises in domestic terms, and the government cannot print foreign currency to repay it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Freya writes: "Expansionary fiscal policy always causes inflation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: If there is a large deflationary gap (horizontal Keynesian AS), higher AD raises output with little effect on the price level.
items.markingKey: If there is a large deflationary gap (horizontal Keynesian AS), higher AD raises output with little effect on the price level. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between direct taxes and indirect taxes.
items.answer: Direct taxes are levied on income and wealth and paid directly by the taxpayer (income tax); indirect taxes are levied on spending and collected through sellers (VAT).
items.markingKey: Direct taxes are levied on income and wealth and paid directly by the taxpayer (income tax); indirect taxes are levied on spending and collected through sellers (VAT). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between crowding out and crowding in.
items.answer: Crowding out is the reduction in private spending caused by government borrowing raising interest rates; crowding in is when government spending, especially on infrastructure in a recession, raises confidence and profitability, increasing private investment.
items.markingKey: Crowding out is the reduction in private spending caused by government borrowing raising interest rates; crowding in is when government spending, especially on infrastructure in a recession, raises confidence and profitability, increasing private investment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why high levels of government debt may reduce future economic growth.
items.answer: Rising interest payments divert spending from productive investment; future tax rises may reduce incentives; markets may demand higher interest rates, crowding out private investment.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rising interest payments divert spending from productive investment; future tax rises may reduce incentives; markets may demand higher interest rates, crowding out private investment. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why a government might use contractionary fiscal policy even though it may increase unemployment.
items.answer: To reduce an inflationary gap or excessive deficits and debt: lower AD reduces inflationary pressure and borrowing, but output and employment fall in the short run.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: To reduce an inflationary gap or excessive deficits and debt: lower AD reduces inflationary pressure and borrowing, but output and employment fall in the short run. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using the UK budget deficit in 2020-21 as an example, explain the government budget and deficits.
items.answer: UK public sector net borrowing reached about 15% of GDP in 2020-21, the highest since the Second World War, because of the furlough scheme and lower tax revenue. A collapse in revenue and large emergency spending created a record peacetime deficit
items.markingKey: Context (UK public sector net borrowing reached about 15% of GDP in 2020-21, the highest since the Second World War, because of the furlough scheme and lower tax revenue.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A collapse in revenue and large emergency spending created a record peacetime deficit – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the government budget and deficits.

items.stem: With reference to the UK's 2022 "mini-budget", explain how it illustrates constraints on fiscal policy.
items.answer: In September 2022 the UK announced £45 bn of unfunded tax cuts; gilt yields rose sharply and the pound fell to a record low against the dollar, and most measures were reversed. Markets' fear about debt sustainability raised borrowing costs, showing that credibility limits expansionary policy
items.markingKey: Context (In September 2022 the UK announced £45 bn of unfunded tax cuts; gilt yields rose sharply and the pound fell to a record low against the dollar, and most measures were reversed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Using the Greek debt crisis as an example, explain consequences of unsustainable government debt.
items.answer: Greek government debt exceeded 170% of GDP by 2011; Greece needed three bailouts (2010, 2012, 2015) and a restructuring that imposed losses of over 50% on private creditors in 2012. Loss of market confidence raised borrowing costs to unaffordable levels, forcing austerity and default
items.markingKey: Context (Greek government debt exceeded 170% of GDP by 2011; Greece needed three bailouts (2010, 2012, 2015) and a restructuring that imposed losses of over 50% on private creditors in 2012.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Loss of market confidence raised borrowing costs to unaffordable levels, forcing austerity and default – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to consequences of unsustainable government debt.

items.stem: Outline one way in which China's 2008 stimulus package shows fiscal policy and AD.
items.answer: In November 2008 China announced a 4 trillion yuan stimulus (about 12% of GDP) focused on infrastructure. Large spending on railways and roads sustained growth above 9% in 2009, though it raised local government debt
items.markingKey: Context (In November 2008 China announced a 4 trillion yuan stimulus (about 12% of GDP) focused on infrastructure.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large spending on railways and roads sustained growth above 9% in 2009, though it raised local government debt – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to fiscal policy and AD.

items.stem: "Transfer payments are counted as government spending (G) in aggregate demand." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Transfers redistribute income and are not payment for current output, so they are excluded from G; they affect AD indirectly through consumption.

items.stem: With reference to Japan's high public debt, explain how it illustrates debt sustainability.
